title: The traveling scholars
hookLine: scholars journeyed far to hear one hadith from its source

cards: One line in Sahih al-Bukhari, almost tucked away in a chapter heading. Jabir ibn Abdullah, a companion of the Prophet ﷺ, traveled a month's distance to Abdullah ibn Unays, for a single hadith. Not for trade.
Not for war. One report. Fuller tellings of the story, outside Bukhari, add the details: Jabir buys a camel, saddles up, and rides to hear the report himself rather than take it secondhand.

teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, in the Book of Knowledge, the chapter on going out in search of knowledge names Jabir's journey, and the report placed beneath it is about a prophet.

Moses went looking for a man with knowledge he didn't have. The Qur'an gives his resolve, in Pickthall's words: "I will not give up until I reach the point where the two rivers meet, though I march on for ages."
A companion and a prophet in one chapter: travel for learning sits in old company.

Why not take it secondhand? Because every link in the chain is a place for something to slip, as the scholars knew. Hear it from the person who heard it, and the chain gets shorter and the path clearer.
Scholars of hadith prized a shorter chain, and some traveled for that alone. The journey became a tradition of its own.
Students moved between cities to sit with the teachers there, to compare what they'd heard, to check a report against another chain.
It even has a name, rihla, and the scholar al-Khatib al-Baghdadi wrote a book gathering these journeys in search of hadith. What did they carry home? Not souvenirs.

And the habit behind them is spelled out in a hadith in Sahih Muslim: whoever travels a road seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a road to paradise. By that hadith, the road to learning is itself counted.

how: Students of hadith and Islamic learning have long traveled to study with teachers in person, a practice called the rihla, and some still travel to receive a chain of transmission directly from a teacher.

games.q: you're Jabir. a companion a month's ride away holds a hadith you've only heard secondhand. what do you do?
o: buy a camel and ride a month to hear it.
write and ask him to send it.
games.why: in the fuller tellings, he bought a camel and rode for a month, for one report, to hear it from the one who held it.

practice: Think of something you've only ever taken secondhand, a question about your faith, your family's history, your work, and ask who holds it firsthand: a teacher, an elder, a grandparent, a scholar at the mosque or the library across town.
Picture the journey, even if it's twenty minutes on a bus or a phone call across an ocean, and the one question you'd bring. If you pray, you can ask for an easy road.

wordCard.voice: The traveling scholars. Companions and students who rode far to hear a report from its source, so the chain would be shorter and surer. Today's word.
